title: Area VI review: Safety and Risk Management
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area VI: weather decisions and icing, loss of control, runway safety, and cockpit technology. Many join two of them in one flight, such as an icing encounter that ends with a stall risk on landing.

questions.q: Your single is not approved for icing and its POH gives no icing speeds. After an inadvertent encounter you still carry rime on the leading edges as you near a 4,000 ft runway. Your normal full-flap approach speed is 65 KIAS and the POH landing distance is 1,300 ft. Which plan fits AC 91-74B?
options: Fly the normal 65 KIAS so the touchdown stays short, then flare as usual
Fly at least 81 KIAS, carry more power, limit the flare, and expect roughly 1,950 ft or more
Fly 60 KIAS to shorten the landing, since the extra drag from the ice will slow you anyway
Fly 81 KIAS, then hold the nose high in a long flare to bleed off the extra speed before touchdown
questions.why: With no icing speed in the AFM, POH or placards, AC 91-74B says to fly at least 25 percent above the normal speed for the flap setting: 65 x 1.25 = 81.25 KIAS. It estimates 20 percent more landing distance for each 10 percent of extra speed, so 25 percent faster is about 50 percent longer: 1,300 x 1.5 = 1,950 ft, and more if the runway is contaminated [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]. Carry more power and limit the flare, because many icing accidents were a stall induced in the flare [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]]. A slow approach is the trap: ice makes the wing stall at a lower angle of attack and a higher airspeed [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11a]], and most icing accidents happen in the final phases of flight [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10d]].

questions.q: You are IFR at 5,000 ft in a single not approved for icing, in rain with the outside air at +3 °C. A warm front lies over your destination, which reports ice pellets at -2 °C. What does that report most likely mean for your descent?
options: Ice pellets are already frozen and bounce off, so they are no icing threat
The icing is only in a thin layer at the surface, so a fast final will get you through it
There is supercooled rain in the cold air between you and the runway; it often covers a broad area and descending may not get you out
Ice pellets mean the freezing level is above you, so your descent will be in warmer air
questions.why: Under a warm front, rain forms in the warm air above the frontal surface, then falls into the cold air below and becomes supercooled. If that cold layer is deep, the drops may freeze into ice pellets, and the AWH says ice pellets indicate icing above [[28:247|AWH 20-5]] [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1l]]. So your descent from +3 °C goes through the very layer where the rain is supercooled. Freezing precipitation often covers a broad area, and a pilot may not escape it by descending [[28:247|AWH 20-5]]. The pellets themselves are not the threat; the freezing rain above them is. Even an airplane approved for known icing is not approved for freezing rain [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2a]].

questions.q: Planning an IFR flight in stratus, you see +9 °C at your departure airport, field elevation 1,000 ft. You want to cruise at 6,000 ft MSL, inside the cloud. Using only the average lapse rate, what do you expect, and what should you do with that estimate?
options: About +3 °C at 6,000 ft, warm enough that icing is unlikely
About -1 °C at 6,000 ft, inside the range where the AIM says to expect icing in visible moisture; check forecast temperatures and freezing levels, since inversions break the average
About -1 °C, but structural ice needs at least -10 °C, so the flight is fine
About -3 °C, which proves the freezing level is at the surface
questions.why: The average lapse rate is 2 °C per 1,000 ft [[1:297|PHAK 12-13]]. 6,000 ft MSL is 5,000 ft above the field, so 9 - (2 x 5) = -1 °C, and the estimated freezing level is near 1,000 + (9 / 2) x 1,000 = 5,500 ft MSL. The AIM says to expect icing in visible precipitation, such as rain or cloud droplets, from +2 to -10 °C [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19b]], and AC 91-74B expects icing in clouds at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]. The average is only a starting point: AC 91-74B says to get the actual freezing levels and to know about inversions and multiple freezing levels [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1c]]. Winds aloft forecasts give the approximate freezing level [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1]].

questions.q: Friday evening you plan a 150 NM VFR trip in marginal weather to a family event on Saturday. Which plan best defends against get-there-itis?
options: Lower your ceiling minimum by 500 ft for this one trip, since you know the route well
Use your written minimums, pick a specific point for the final continue or divert decision, list an alternate about every 25 to 30 NM (5 or 6 here), and tell the family you may be late or divert
Plan to climb on top if it closes in, and ask ATC for help finding a hole at the destination
Give the family an exact arrival time so you stay focused on the schedule
questions.why: The RMH says not to adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight; written minimums make a no-go or divert decision easier and help explain it to passengers [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. The PHAK's mitigations include a reasonable alternate for every 25 to 30 NM of the route in marginal weather (150 / 30 = 5 and 150 / 25 = 6), preparing passengers for delay and diversion [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]], and choosing a specific place for the final continue or divert decision [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]]. The RMH says to tell people waiting for you that you need flexibility [[30:40|RMH 5-2]]. Going on top hoping for a hole or for ATC to talk you down is an AC 91-92 Don't [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. A fixed arrival time feeds the fixation on the destination that defines get-there-itis [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

questions.q: At night you fly a visual approach in light rain and haze to an unfamiliar runway with no glide path lights. Rain streams on the windscreen and the runway looks far away, so you feel high and want to push over. What is going on, and what is the safe response?
options: You really are high; both cues confirm it, so steepen the descent
Rain makes you feel higher and haze makes the runway look farther away, so both push you low; hold a constant glide path and go around if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft
Haze makes you feel lower, so you should shallow the approach
Rain and haze have no effect at night because the runway lights are bright
questions.why: The AIM says rain on the windscreen can create the illusion of greater height and haze the illusion of greater distance, and a pilot who does not recognize them flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5b3(e)]]. The fix is to fly the stabilized approach, a constant glide path, typically 3 degrees, to the touchdown zone [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. In the pattern, an approach that becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL calls for an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. AC 91-92 adds to allow more margin at night, when clouds and the horizon may be hard or impossible to see [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

questions.q: You are a VFR-only pilot at 5,500 ft over a broken layer that is filling in below you. Your destination, 80 NM ahead, is forecast to improve by your arrival. The airport 15 NM behind you is VFR. What do AC 91-92 and the RMH point to?
options: Continue on top; the forecast says the destination will improve
Continue, and if it is overcast at the destination ask ATC to talk you down
Turn back while you are still in VMC and land at the airport behind you
Descend through the first gap you find and scud run under the layer
questions.why: AC 91-92 lists as Don'ts proceeding on top hoping to find a hole at the other end or hoping ATC will talk you down, and continuing VFR into IMC. Its advice is to wait it out or turn around [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]]. In the RMH vacuum-pump case, the pilot could have changed the outcome by diverting while still in VMC [[30:12|RMH 1-3]]. Scud running, staying low to keep the ground in sight while instrument conditions exist, is a PHAK operational pitfall [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]], and the RMH lists continued VFR into low ceilings or visibility as a common path to controlled flight into terrain [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

questions.q: IFR in a single not approved for icing, the autopilot is holding altitude while light rime builds. Over 10 minutes the airspeed slowly drops from 120 to 85 KIAS at the same power. What is the danger, and what should you do?
options: None yet; the autopilot will warn you before anything goes wrong
The autopilot is raising the angle of attack to hold altitude and may mask the stall cues; disconnect it, fly by hand, keep the airspeed up, and exit the icing now, declaring an emergency
Trim nose-up to help the autopilot hold altitude until you reach the destination
Wait for an ATC clearance to a new altitude before you change anything
questions.why: Ice adds drag, which shows up as lost airspeed; with limited power the airplane may soon approach the stall [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-3]]. AC 61-67C warns that an autopilot may mask the tactile stall cues or try to fly the airplane in the stall, and a sudden disconnect with the trim at an extreme setting complicates recovery [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102c]]. In an airplane not approved for icing, stall warning will most likely not work in ice [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c(2)]]. AC 91-74B says to exit as expeditiously as possible and declare an emergency, and not to wait for a clearance that may not come in time [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. The RMH notes a pilot used to the autopilot may be unprepared when it disconnects in icing [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: Your airplane stalls at 52 KIAS at 1 G. Low over a ridge, you pull hard at 85 KIAS to clear rising terrain, loading the airplane to 3 G. What happens?
options: Nothing; 85 KIAS is well above the 52 KIAS stall speed
It can stall: at 3 G the stall speed is about 90 KIAS, so you are in an accelerated stall
It can stall only if the bank is more than 60 degrees
Stall speed falls as you climb, so the pull is safe
questions.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]]: 52 x the square root of 3 = 52 x 1.732 = about 90 KIAS, which is above your 85 KIAS. A stall at a higher airspeed from maneuvering loads is an accelerated stall [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]]; it tends to be more aggressive and can lead to a spin if not recovered at once [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Bank is only one way to add load. Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100j]]. An abrupt pull on the elevator near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

questions.q: A tailwind on base carries you past the centerline of a short runway. You are at 30 degrees of bank, the nose is coming around too slowly, and you are tempted to add left (inside) rudder and pull. What is the risk, and the fix?
options: A slipping stall that spins to the right; hold opposite aileron
A skidding cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin, usually toward the rudder you applied (left); go around instead
No real risk below 45 degrees of bank; skid to save the landing
A spiral dive; reduce power and keep the turn going
questions.why: The AFH describes this exact setup: an unnoticed tailwind on base, an overshoot, then more bank, more back pressure and inside rudder. The bank tends to increase, the nose drops, the pilot pulls, and a stall with these inputs can rapidly become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A spin from a cross-controlled stall usually rotates in the direction of the rudder being applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]], here to the left. The AFH says the safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around, to be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees of bank low in the pattern, and never to skid to correct [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A slip with opposite aileron spins the other way, but that is not what this pilot is doing [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

questions.q: Going around from a short final at 150 ft AGL, you add full power with the trim still set for approach. The nose rises, the airspeed sags and the stall horn sounds. The ground is close. What first?
options: Pull back to stop the sink, since you are close to the ground
Hold the attitude and let full power fly you out of it
Push forward to lower the angle of attack until the warning stops, with right rudder, then climb at a safe attitude
Raise all the flaps at once to cut drag
questions.why: The most important action for an impending or full stall is to reduce the angle of attack. The AFH notes many cases where pilots put power and altitude first instead, and lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Power reduces the altitude lost but does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. On a go-around, full power with approach trim raises the nose and yaws left; letting the nose rise too early can cause an unrecoverable stall at low altitude, so expect strong forward pressure and right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. A sudden full flap retraction can make the airplane settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: Your airplane stalls with a wing drop and begins to rotate. The slip/skid ball is pinned to the left, and the turn coordinator's airplane symbol shows a turn to the right. Which rudder do you apply?
options: Left rudder, away from the ball
Right rudder, toward the turn indication
Left rudder, opposite the turn coordinator's indication of rotation to the right
No rudder; neutralize all controls and wait
questions.why: In a spin, use the turn indicator's symbolic airplane for the direction of rotation, not the ball. The ball moves according to where it is mounted: one on the left side always goes left, even in a spin to the right [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Rotation is to the right, so apply full left rudder, opposite the rotation, and start the incipient spin recovery before 360 degrees of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Apply it briskly and hold it; slow, cautious rudder can let the spin go on [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Power goes to idle and the ailerons to neutral first [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

questions.q: You fly solo with half fuel in moderate turbulence toward a gusty airport. The POH lists maneuvering speed as 105 KIAS at maximum gross weight. Which statement is right?
options: At your light weight, VA is above 105 KIAS, so cruise at 110 KIAS
At your light weight, VA is below 105 KIAS; slow well below 105 in the turbulence, and fly a higher than normal approach speed in the gusts
Weight has no effect on VA, and gusts never affect stall speed
Fly the approach slower than normal so a gust cannot overstress the airplane
questions.why: AC 61-67C says maneuvering speed is lower at a lower weight, and in moderate or severe turbulence you should fly well above stall speed and below maneuvering speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]]. Full or abrupt control movements are not for speeds at or above VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100f]]. A vertical gust or wind shear can raise the angle of attack suddenly, so the airplane may stall at a much higher airspeed while you fight for the flightpath, which is why AC 61-67C calls for a higher than normal approach speed in moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]].

questions.q: Your newly bought single has an unheated AOA indicator. After picking up some ice on a winter flight, the indicator shows a comfortable margin on final. How much should you trust it?
options: Fully; an AOA indicator measures the real stall margin whatever the airspeed
Not fully: wing contamination and unheated vanes are listed limits, and ice makes the wing stall at a lower angle of attack, so fly the icing speeds and treat the margin with doubt
Fully, as long as the stall warning horn is also silent
Not at all; AOA indicators are not useful in light airplanes
questions.why: The AFH lists what limits an AOA indicator, including calibration, unheated probes or vanes, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:119|AFH 5-14]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A wing with ice ordinarily stalls at a lower AOA and so a higher airspeed [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11a]], and contamination can bring a stall with few of the usual cues, including the warning horn [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102a]]. AOA indicators are useful: the FAA promotes them to cut loss of control accidents, and you should learn how yours works and practice with it [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: Your POH gives 1,250 ft to land over a 50 ft obstacle, dry and with no margin added. On arrival the ATIS reports runway condition codes 3/3/3 for the 3,800 ft runway (more than 1/8 inch of wet snow), and you have no other data. Using AC 91-79B Table 3-1, what do you do?
options: Land: 1,250 x 1.67 = about 2,090 ft
Land: 1,250 ft plus 15 percent is about 1,440 ft
Do not land there: 1,250 x 3.2 = 4,000 ft, more than the 3,800 ft available
Do not land there: 1,250 x 3.2 x 1.15 = 4,600 ft is needed
questions.why: With no manufacturer or data provider figures, multiply the dry, unfactored POH distance by the Table 3-1 factor for the conditions on arrival [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. Code 3 (medium braking) is 3.2 for a reciprocating airplane [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]; more than 1/8 inch of wet snow is a code 3 condition [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]]. 1,250 x 3.2 = 4,000 ft, which is more than 3,800 ft, so the runway fails. The factors already include the 15 percent margin, so do not add it again (that gives the wrong 4,600 ft) [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.3.3]]. The 1.67 factor is for a dry runway (code 6). Except in an emergency, do not land on a runway that fails the assessment [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]].

questions.q: Your POH landing distance over 50 ft is 1,350 ft, dry. You are high on short final to a dry 2,300 ft runway and will cross the threshold at about 90 ft. Using AC 91-79B's rules of thumb, what is the best call?
options: Land: 40 ft high adds only about 80 ft
Land: about 2,150 ft is needed and the runway is 2,300 ft
Go around: about 2,150 ft is needed, and with the 15 percent margin that is about 2,470 ft, more than the runway
Dive for the numbers to lose the extra height
questions.why: AFM landing distances assume 50 ft over the threshold, and each 10 ft higher adds about 200 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]: (90 - 50) / 10 x 200 = 800 ft, so 1,350 + 800 = 2,150 ft. AC 91-79B says to add a margin of at least 15 percent to the operational landing distance and not to land on a runway that fails it, except in an emergency [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]: 2,150 x 1.15 = about 2,470 ft, more than 2,300 ft. A dive to fix it adds speed, and 10 percent fast adds about 20 percent [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. A very high approach that cannot be stabilized normally ends in a go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: Ground control says, "Cessna 45K, taxi to Runway 27 via Alpha, hold short of Runway 32." Which reply fits the AIM and AC 91-73B?
options: "Wilco, 5K."
"Roger, Cessna 45K."
"Runway 27 via Alpha, hold short Runway 32, Cessna 45K."
"Taxi via Alpha, Cessna 45K."
questions.why: Read back the runway assignment and any instruction to hold short of a runway [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]. AC 91-73B says to include the complete call sign and the runway designator in readbacks of hold short and runway entry instructions, and to avoid "Roger" or "Wilco" for them [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]]. Since many incursions happen even after a correct hold short readback, it also suggests a physical reminder, such as something hung on the yoke [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(3)]]. ATC gives hold short instructions or crossing clearances for runways along the route, and a taxi instruction to Runway 27 does not authorize entering or crossing Runway 27 itself at any point [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]].

questions.q: After landing at a towered airport you turn off onto a taxiway. Your main wheels are past the runway holding position markings, but the tail is still over them. You want to raise the flaps and switch to ground. Tower has said nothing more. What now?
options: Stop here and do the flaps and radios; the main wheels are clear
Keep taxiing until every part of the airplane has crossed the markings, then hold and do the after-landing items
Turn onto the parallel runway to make room for the airplane behind you
Stop on the runway side of the line until tower tells you where to go
questions.why: An airplane exiting a runway is not clear until all parts of it have crossed the holding position marking [[33:151|AIM 2-3-5a1]]. Without other instructions, taxi beyond the markings, then hold unless ATC gives more instructions [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21b]]. AC 91-73B says to change nothing, such as flaps, trim or radios, until the whole airplane has crossed the landing runway's hold short line [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]]. Do not exit onto another runway unless ATC authorizes it [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21a]].

questions.q: You fly an instrument approach in IMC. Everything is on speed and on path, but you are slow getting configured, and the landing flaps are not set until 800 ft above the airport. By the AFH guidance, what should you do?
options: Continue: you were stabilized by 500 ft
Continue, because the flaps were set before 300 ft
Go around: in IMC the approach should be stabilized by 1,000 ft above the airport, and it was not
Continue, but add 10 knots to make up for the late flaps
questions.why: Landing flaps as required are one of the AFH stabilized approach elements [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. The AFH says pilots typically go around if not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC or 1,000 ft in IMC; the 300 ft AGL gate is for a typical piston airplane in a VFR traffic pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. 800 ft is below the IMC gate. Adding speed is not a fix: the stabilized band is +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and 10 percent fast adds about 20 percent to the landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

questions.q: Your main tires are inflated to 30 psi. Heavy rain is falling on a smooth runway, and your normal touchdown speed is about 55 knots. What is true?
options: Dynamic hydroplaning is possible from about 47 knots, so you touch down above that speed; touch down as slowly as safety allows, brake moderately, and expect it may continue below 47
Hydroplaning starts only above about 258 knots, so it cannot happen to a light airplane
Hydroplaning cannot start unless the runway is reported as code 0
Lock the brakes at touchdown so the tires cut through the water
questions.why: Minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed is about 8.6 times the square root of the tire pressure in psi [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]: 8.6 x the square root of 30 = 8.6 x 5.48 = about 47 knots, below your 55 knot touchdown. Once started it may persist to a much slower speed [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]. In moderate or heavy rain on a smooth runway, assume the water may be deeper than 1/8 inch [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.5.2]]. The AFH says to use a grooved runway if there is one, touch down as slowly as safety allows, lower the nose and brake moderately, and release the brakes at the first sign of a skid [[24:209|AFH 9-38]]. A long locked-wheel skid causes reverted rubber hydroplaning [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]. (258 is 8.6 x 30, without the square root.)

questions.q: Your tablet's moving map database expired two cycles ago. You plan a VFR flight that passes close to a Class B shelf. What do the AIM and PHAK say?
options: It is illegal to fly VFR with an out-of-date database
It is fine: the database need not be current for VFR, so no extra checks are needed
There is no VFR rule requiring an update, but do not rely on the outdated map around critical airspace; check the airspace and waypoints against current charts
Only the approach charts expire; airspace on a moving map never changes
questions.why: The AIM says databases must be updated for IFR and should be updated for all other use, but there is no requirement for VFR. It does not recommend using a moving map with an outdated database in and around critical airspace, and says to verify waypoints with current products such as the sectional chart or Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]]. The PHAK adds that without a current database the map should be disregarded for critical navigation decisions [[1:419|PHAK 16-32]]. Databases are updated every 28 days [[23:30|IFH 1-11]].

questions.q: IFR in cruise in your own airplane, the VOR needle starts to wander soon after a passenger turns on a laptop hotspot and you plug a new USB charger into your tablet. What is the best course?
options: Ignore it; 91.21 covers only airline flights
Keep flying the airplane, isolate the devices one at a time while you watch the needle, note the conditions, and turn off the one causing it
Turn off all aircraft radios to stop the interference
Ask ATC whether the devices are allowed
questions.why: Under IFR, 91.21 bars any PED unless the operator has determined it will not interfere with navigation or communication, and in a non-certificate-holder aircraft the PIC may make that determination [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. AC 91.21-1D says that if interference appears, isolate the devices causing it, record the conditions, and turn the device off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]]. The rule covers every aircraft operated under IFR, not only airlines [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. Any PED, including your tablet, should be evaluated by the user or operator so it will not interfere [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]].

questions.q: On autopilot in NAV mode tracking GPS, you switch the e-HSI navigation source to LOC to fly the localizer. Shortly after, the airplane holds wings level and flies straight through the localizer. What most likely happened?
options: The localizer signal failed
Changing the source dropped NAV mode, so the autopilot went to ROL (wings level); reengage NAV or the approach mode and verify the mode annunciation
The autopilot is waiting for the glideslope before it turns
The GPS lost RAIM and the autopilot disconnected
questions.why: The PHAK warns that with some autopilots, changing the e-HSI source from GPS to LOC or VOR while in NAV mode disengages NAV, and lateral control defaults to ROL (wings level) until the pilot reengages NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. The pilot needs to know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify that armed functions engage [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. That is the RMH loop of anticipate, act, verify for every button push [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. If the automation is not doing what you expect, reduce the level of automation and fly manually while you sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: You are buying a fixed-gear, 180 hp tailwheel airplane with a glass PFD, an MFD with a GPS moving map and a two-axis autopilot. You have flown only nosewheel airplanes. Which logbook endorsement does 61.31 require before you act as PIC?
options: A tailwheel endorsement, plus a TAA endorsement for the glass panel
Only a tailwheel endorsement; there is no 61.31 endorsement for glass panels or autopilots, though transition training on them is recommended
A high-performance endorsement and a tailwheel endorsement
None, if you hold a commercial or ATP certificate
questions.why: 61.31(i) requires logged flight training in a tailwheel airplane and an endorsement, unless you logged tailwheel PIC time before April 15, 1991 [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(i)]]. High-performance means more than 200 hp, so 180 hp does not need one [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. Part 61 defines a TAA [[60:187|14 CFR 61.1(b)]], but 61.31 has no glass panel endorsement. AC 61-98E says pilots moving to a TAA should get specialized transition training from an instructor with that equipment [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]]. The 61.31 endorsements apply whatever certificate you hold.

questions.q: Before a long night VFR trip, you load a direct GPS route on your tablet. The straight line crosses high terrain and passes near restricted airspace. Which habit do the PHAK and AIM recommend?
options: Follow the magenta line; the moving map shows everything you need
Check the programmed route on the ground against a paper log, and if they differ do not assume the computer is right; plan a realistic route
Program a new route in flight once you see the terrain
Use the moving map as your primary terrain reference at night
questions.why: The PHAK warns that a pilot who only follows the magenta line can fly into high terrain or prohibited airspace [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. It says to check all programming before departure, compare the route with a paper log, and if they do not match, not to assume the computer is correct, and to plan a realistic route [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. AFMs prohibit using moving map and terrain displays as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. The AIM says VFR waypoints should be loaded on the ground and pilots should avoid programming routes in flight [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17b1(e)(5)]].
